quests.hint: Where sick people are treated. It has three syllables, and the vowel in the middle is a weak one.
quests.explanation: Hos-pi-tal: the middle vowel is weak in speech but is written i, and the ending is -al, not -el or -le. The word shares its Latin source with hotel and hostel.

quests.hint: Not easy. It has a double consonant in the first syllable.
quests.explanation: Dif-fi-cult has ff, because the prefix dis- becomes dif- before f, as in different. The word ends in -cult, with no e.

quests.hint: It keeps the rain off. Three syllables, with a double letter near the end.
quests.explanation: Um-brel-la: a b sits after the m and a double l follows. Say each chunk slowly, and the ending -ella comes into view.

quests.hint: Where you live, or to speak to someone. It has two doubled letters.
quests.explanation: Ad-dress: the dd comes from the prefix ad- meeting dress, and the ss is at the end. Both doubles are real, so 'adress' is wrong.

quests.hint: The courses a school teaches. It has a double r near the start.
quests.explanation: Cur-ric-u-lum has rr after the first syllable, and it ends in -um, as in a Latin word. The plural is curricula.

quests.hint: The way you think and feel about something. It begins with a doubled consonant.
quests.explanation: At-ti-tude has tt in the middle and ends in -tude, as in gratitude and altitude. The -tude ending is easy to write as -tood.

quests.hint: A female child. The gh is silent, and the vowel sounds like /ɔː/.
quests.explanation: The letters augh say /ɔː/ in daughter, caught and taught, and the gh is not pronounced. That group has to be learned as a unit.

quests.hint: The past tense of 'think', and also an idea. The ending says /ɔːt/.
quests.explanation: Thought uses ough for /ɔː/, as in bought and brought. This is different from though and through, which you have already practised.

quests.hint: Not curved. The long a is spelled with a four-letter group.
quests.explanation: Straight has aigh for /eɪ/, which is unusual. Do not confuse it with 'strait', a narrow channel, which sounds the same.

quests.hint: English is one. There is a u after the g, and it is not 'langwidge'.
quests.explanation: Lan-guage: gu keeps the g hard before a, as in guard and guarantee. The ending -uage is /wɪdʒ/, so 'langage' loses the u.

quests.hint: A small baked snack. Say it BIS-kit, but write it with an extra pair of vowels.
quests.explanation: Bis-cuit ends in -cuit, said /kɪt/. The word came from French, and the odd u-i order is a leftover of that origin.

quests.hint: A stringed instrument. There is a u after the g, but you don't say it, and the stress falls on the second syllable.
quests.explanation: Gu-itar: the silent u keeps the g hard before i, as in guilty and guide. The stress is on -tar, and the ending is -ar.

quests.hint: Something unexpected. It ends in a /z/ sound but is not written with z.
quests.explanation: Surprise ends in -ise in every variety of English. A small group of verbs, including advertise and exercise, are always -ise, never -ize.

quests.hint: Physical activity. The c after the x is soft, and the ending has a /z/ sound.
quests.explanation: Ex-er-cise has a soft c before i, as in city, and it ends in -cise. There is no -ize form in any spelling system.

quests.hint: To promote a product. The stressed part comes at the beginning, and the ending is -ise.
quests.explanation: Ad-ver-tise is spelled -ise in both British and American English, so 'advertize' is wrong in both. It belongs with surprise and exercise.

quests.hint: Where you learn. The opening /sk/ is written with three letters.
quests.explanation: The letters sch say /sk/ in school, scheme and scholar. This comes from Greek, and the vowel is oo, as in moon.

quests.hint: The science of substances. The first syllable starts with /k/ but not with c or k.
quests.explanation: In Greek-derived words, ch says /k/: chemistry, chorus, character. The middle syllable is -is-, not -es-, as in the base 'chemist'.

quests.hint: A device with moving parts. The first sound is /ʃ/ written with ch, and the last is /iːn/.
quests.explanation: Ma-chine is French in origin, and it keeps the French ch for /ʃ/ and -ine for /iːn/. The same -ine says /iːn/ in magazine and routine.

quests.hint: A huge grey animal with a trunk. The /f/ sound is not written with f.
quests.explanation: El-e-phant has ph for /f/. This is Greek in origin, and it also appears in alphabet and photograph. The ending is -ant.

quests.hint: The letters from a to z. It is named after the first two letters of the Greek writing system.
quests.explanation: Alpha + bet: the word is named from alpha and beta, and ph says /f/. The middle a is weak, so be sure it is written.

quests.hint: A picture taken by a camera. It is built from Greek roots meaning 'light' and 'writing'.
quests.explanation: Photo (light) + graph (write): ph appears twice, both saying /f/. The root graph is also found in paragraph and biography.

quests.hint: Fair and sensible. The base word is 'reason', followed by a common adjective ending.
quests.explanation: Reason + able: the full base word keeps every letter, and -able attaches to it. This is the more productive of the two endings.

quests.hint: Showing good judgement. Although 'sense' is a word, the ending is not the one you might expect.
quests.explanation: Sensible ends in -ible, even though sense is a real word. It comes from Latin sensibilis, so it does not follow the -able pattern.

quests.hint: Able to bend or adapt. The base 'flex' is a word, but the ending is the less common one.
quests.explanation: Flexible has -ible, although flex is a complete word. The ending follows the Latin flexibilis, so sound alone will not settle it.

quests.hint: Something you own. It has two pairs of doubled letters.
quests.explanation: Pos-ses-sion has ss twice, once after each vowel: possess + ion. One s in the middle gives 'posession'.

quests.hint: Correct in every detail. It starts with a double consonant.
quests.explanation: Ac-cu-rate has cc: the first c says /k/ and the second says /k/ too. The ending -ate is weak, /ət/.

quests.hint: An idea offered to someone. It has a double g in the middle.
quests.explanation: Sug-ges-tion has gg because the prefix sub- changes to sug- before g. The ending -stion says /stʃən/, as in question.

quests.hint: All the words you know. It has five syllables and ends in a weak -ary.
quests.explanation: Vo-cab-u-lar-y ends in -ary, as in dictionary and necessary. The fourth chunk is -lar-, with an a; 'vocabulery' is wrong.

quests.hint: To admit or recognise something. A silent letter sits after the c, and the ending is -edge.
quests.explanation: Ac-knowl-edge has a silent k, as in know, sitting after c. The word ends in -edge, as in knowledge.

quests.hint: Your inner sense of right and wrong. It contains the word 'science' inside it.
quests.explanation: Con-science has sci inside it, and sc says /ʃ/ here. The word comes from Latin, and both con- and science are visible in the spelling.
